planting.note: Direct sow in fall on a lean, fast-draining slope; resist the urge to amend the soil or baby it with water, since this species thrives on neglect and rots with regular irrigation.

directions: One of the toughest, most reliable California natives, this shrub blooms nearly year-round with bright yellow flowers, tolerates terrible soil including alkaline, decomposed granite, and salty ground, and is a magnet for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. The puffy seed pods persist attractively after bloom and can be left for winter interest or collected for easy reseeding. Prune lightly after the main bloom flush to keep the naturally sprawling habit tidy; it rebounds quickly and is deer resistant.

planting.note: Plant cutting-grown stock of known sex in fall around a pond edge or bioswale; cut back hard every few years to prevent legginess.

directions: A fast-growing, cold-hardy baccharis for riparian and bioswale plantings, this shrub fills a niche between coastal and desert-wash species, pairing well with sedges, rushes, and desert willow. Because it tolerates both drought and regular moisture, it is more forgiving of mixed-irrigation zones than most chaparral shrubs. Female plants produce showy white seed-fluff in fall that is attractive but can self-sow aggressively in moist sites.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in fall under oaks or on shaded north slopes; avoid summer water once established, since root rot is the primary failure mode.

directions: A shade-tolerant evergreen with distinctive pendant tassel flowers and glossy leaves, this silktassel is valuable as an understory or woodland-edge shrub where few broadleaf evergreens handle dry shade, and its berries feed birds and mammals through winter. Site it under oaks or on shaded north slopes where its drought tolerance and shade tolerance combine to fill a gap most natives cannot. The dioecious flowers mean growing both sexes nearby maximizes the ornamental winter berry display.

planting.note: Direct sow with stratification into sharply drained chaparral soil in full sun; give complete summer drought once established.

directions: A sun-loving, small-tree-like silktassel for Southern California chaparral gardens, this species offers year-round tassel bloom and a dense evergreen form distinct from the more commonly grown coastal silktassel. It can be limbed up into a small multi-trunk tree form or left dense as a background hedge. It is adapted to fire-prone slopes and resents any supplemental irrigation beyond the first year or two.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into sandy or decomposed-granite soil with rapid drainage; essentially no irrigation after the first summer.

directions: Filling the desert and high-desert transition niche between coastal and low-desert brittlebush species, this shrub carries silvery foliage and cheerful yellow daisy flowers on a tidy mound, excellent for habitat restoration and pollinator gardens on fast-draining soils. Shear lightly after the spring and summer bloom flush to maintain a compact silvery mound and prevent the woody, open habit it develops if left unpruned. It is an outstanding nurse plant for desert pollinator gardens and tolerates the high heat and cold-winter swings typical of the Mojave-transition zones.

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-treat seed before fall sowing into fast, lean, serpentine or gabbro-derived soil; source only from reputable native nurseries given its conservation status.

directions: A genuinely rare, low-mounding flannelbush native to gabbro soils near Pine Hill, El Dorado County, this federally endangered species offers the same showy yellow flannel-flower display as the more common upright flannelbush already in cultivation but in a compact, spreading form suited to small gardens or rock gardens, supporting numerous specialist native bees. It must have fast, lean drainage and will not tolerate heavy clay or regular irrigation. Its naturally low, spreading habit makes it useful as a specimen on a sunny bank where the upright common flannelbush would be too large.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto a rocky, well-drained slope mimicking coastal chaparral; avoid summer water once established to prevent root rot.

directions: A coastal-bluff and rocky-slope endemic valuable for pollinator-focused gardens, this shrub is documented supporting dozens of native bee, butterfly, and moth species, an unusually high wildlife count for a shrub this size. It is dioecious like other baccharis — only female plants bear the showy cream seed-fluff — so include both sexes if that late-season display is wanted. Its dense habit and heavy wildlife visitation make it an excellent anchor shrub for a coastal pollinator garden.

planting.note: Direct sow or divide rhizomes in fall into a stream edge, bioswale bottom, or seasonal marsh; give it room or contain it, since it spreads readily by rhizome.

directions: Unlike the upland and chaparral baccharis species already in cultivation, this is a true wetland rhizomatous shrub for pond edges, rain gardens, and salt marsh restoration, supporting an exceptional range of native bee and butterfly species. This is the baccharis to use where the site is genuinely wet, rather than the typical dry-chaparral siting other species in the genus need. The dense cream-brown flower clusters bloom nearly year-round and make it one of the highest-value wildlife plants in the genus for a wetland garden.
